transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-21 16:00 UTC
Duration: 1:14
Attendees: Alice Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Priya Patel (Novaterra SRE), Tom Müller (Novaterra Head of Platform), Sara Lopez (Novaterra CTO)

[00:00] Alice Chen: hey everyone, thanks for jumping on, i think we have about an hour, hour fifteen. quick agenda, walk through the on-call playbook for region prioritization, then deep dive into the k v cache healing flows, and a quick convo on batching/quant tradeoffs for private clusters.
[00:22] Priya Patel: yeah thanks Alice. i want to make sure we focus on the runbook for when a region degrades — our ops team got burned last month when an east-1 outage caused weird cache thrash.
[00:35] Diego Ramos: got it. i'll start with an overview of how redwood routes requests across regions today, and then we'll sketch the playbook. so, at a high level we support policy routing: you can set latency-first, cost-first, or capacity-first. policies can be per-tenant or per-route.
[01:02] Tom Müller: quick clar — does policy routing respect sticky sessions / session affinity? our product has sticky contexts for a subset of endpoints.
[01:15] Diego Ramos: good question. there is a sticky option — we call it session affinity — default is stateless routing but you can enable affinity which pins a user to a regional variant until TTL expiry or explicit eviction. note: affinity complicates failover because you may need to prime the kv cache in the fallback region.
[01:39] Sara Lopez: that cache priming bit is what hit us. when east-1 dropped we failed over to eu-west and response times spiked because the k v cache wasn't warmed.
[01:50] Alice Chen: okay let's walk through the 'cache healing' flow. Diego?
[01:56] Diego Ramos: sure. we treat kv cache as lightweight ephemeral state; on failover we have three mitigation stages: 1) passive warmup — the new region gradually warms from live traffic, 2) proactive warming — you can configure prefix prefill (batch replay) for critical prefixes, and 3) snapshot restore — for private deployments we support periodic KV snapshots to S3/KMS and can restore to the fallback region within the window.
[02:26] Priya Patel: snapshot restore — how long does that take for our footprint? we have ~1.2TB of kv entries for active sessions.
[02:36] Diego Ramos: restores for that size are non-trivial; depending on I/O and infra it could be 20-40 minutes to complete a full restore. that's why we usually prefer proactive warming for hot prefixes. snapshot + index shaving can reduce the window. also note quantized model state isn't stored in KV — that's model weights, handled differently.
[02:58] Tom Müller: when you say "proactive warming" is that an automated job we can run during a canary? or do we need to script it?
[03:09] Diego Ramos: both options exist — you can trigger a prefill job from the console or call the API. for private deployments we often ship a playbook script that toggles traffic, runs a warmup job for top-n prefixes, then ramps up real traffic.
[03:29] Priya Patel: can the warmup job replay anonymized user prefixes or do we need synthetic traffic? we can't send PII across regions.
[03:39] Diego Ramos: yes, we support prefix canonicalization — you can map real prefixes to anonymized tokens so the warmup still matches hot states without exposing PII. that's a config in the prefill job.
[03:50] Alice Chen: good. next, eviction and priority — how do we ensure critical routes keep cache after failover?
[03:58] Diego Ramos: two levers: reserve capacity and pinning. reserve capacity is a regional config to keep a percent of KV memory reserved for priority routes; pinning tags specific prefixes to be protected from eviction. pinning is recommended for fewer than ~10k prefixes — beyond that it's less effective.
[04:20] Tom Müller: what's the tradeoff for reserve capacity vs cost?
[04:25] Diego Ramos: reserve capacity reduces effective cache utilization — you run more instances or bigger instances to compensate. so there's a linear cost delta. we can model this for Novaterra: if you reserve 10% across three regions, we'll estimate the extra vram/cost.
[04:40] Priya Patel: i'd like to see that model. our current p95 is 180ms, p99 420ms, the spike went to >1s.
[04:51] Alice Chen: action item to share an impact model — Diego will produce a cost/latency delta table.
[04:58] Diego Ramos: noted. moving on: routing priority during DR. we recommend a tiered policy: first try same-region, then geo-preferred (same continent), then capacity-fallback, and finally cold-fallback to hosted smaller models. you can tune thresholds by CPU/GPU load and p95 latency.
[05:25] Sara Lopez: do you have automated routing thresholds or is that manual?
[05:30] Diego Ramos: you can do both. thresholds can be static or dynamic — we support autoscaling signals to advertise capacity and dynamic routing that will avoid regions with sustained p95 > configured threshold.
[05:44] Tom Müller: what about model variants — do you fall back to quantized variants automatically?
[05:50] Diego Ramos: we support model variants. policy can say "if latency > X, route to quantized variant" — that's helpful to keep latency SLOs at the expense of quality. but note: quantized variants may have longer warmup because kernels differ; in some cases the KV usage pattern changes.
[06:09] Priya Patel: that warmup note — can quantization change cache hit rates?
[06:14] Diego Ramos: yes, subtle differences in tokenization or output structure can change prefix distribution, which impacts cache hits. we advise running a small AB with production prompts to measure.
[06:25] Alice Chen: ok to switch topics briefly — VPC/on-prem constraints? Priya, you had some requirements?
[06:32] Priya Patel: yes. we require that control plane is separated; we accept a private control plane but the inference plane will be in our VPC. we need KMS integration and audit logs forwarded to our SIEM. also, on-call engineers must be able to run diagnostics without exposing secrets.
[06:46] Diego Ramos: for private we support a customer-managed control plane and HSM/KMS integrations (we use standard KMIP endpoints). audit logs can be streamed to syslog or cloud SIEM via secure forwarders. diagnostics are role-gated — we provide ephemeral tokens with limited scopes for SREs.
[07:04] Sara Lopez: what's the rollback plan if a restore attempt makes things worse?
[07:10] Diego Ramos: our playbook includes canary restore: restore to a staging cluster first and run smoke prompts, then flip traffic. if restore causes regressions we have an automated rollback and we keep old snapshots for quick rehydrate.
[07:23] Priya Patel: how do you ensure determinism for prompts during smoke tests? some of our prompts are time-sensitive.
[07:31] Diego Ramos: we have a replay harness that can run with fixed seeds and deterministic model flags where supported. for non-deterministic models we focus on latency and error rates rather than exact match.
[07:44] Alice Chen: let's talk on-call playbook steps — i want concrete steps we can paste into our incident runbook. Diego, can you propose a 6-step playbook?
[07:54] Diego Ramos: sure, rough draft: 1) Detect and classify: auto-alert on region p95/p99 and capacity metrics, 2) Isolate: remove ingress from region if network flapping, 3) Failover: apply priority routing policy (geo-preferred -> capacity fallback), 4) Warm-up: trigger prefix prefill for top-k prefixes and monitor kv-hit rates, 5) Restore: if snapshot strategy is selected, run canary restore to staging, 6) Postmortem: collect traces, cost delta analysis, and update playbook.
[08:26] Tom Müller: can we include run commands for each step? our on-call need one-click runbooks.
[08:33] Diego Ramos: yes we can provide a CLI/playbook script that maps to console actions; we'll share a repo snippet.
[08:40] Priya Patel: concerned about false positives triggering global failover — can you throttle or add human confirm? we had an automated failover triggered by transient cloud control plane latency.
[08:51] Diego Ramos: absolutely. you can require manual approval for global failover or set multi-signal thresholds (e.g., p99 + instance loss > 20%). also support a dry-run where policy is evaluated but not applied.
[09:06] Alice Chen: good — that addresses ops safety. now a short section on batching and quantization tradeoffs for private clusters — Diego?
[09:15] Diego Ramos: batching increases throughput but adds latency; depending on your workload distribution we recommend time-based batching windows for interactive endpoints (e.g., 8-12ms windows) and size-based for high-throughput backends. quantization reduces memory footprint and can increase throughput, but on certain HW the kernel paths for quantized models are less mature and can increase per-token latency for short sequences. so for low-latency interactive apps, measure carefully.
[09:46] Tom Müller: do you have guidance for batch size defaults on A100 vs H100?
[09:51] Diego Ramos: rough defaults: H100 can sustain larger batch sizes (2-3x A100) for FP16/INT8 paths before latency degrades; we'll provide a model-specific table for your models.
[10:02] Priya Patel: ok — we'd like a bench that runs our prompt set with different batch windows and quant levels. can you take that on?
[10:09] Diego Ramos: yes we'll run a bench in our dedicated infra and share CSV output.
[10:14] Alice Chen: quick note on observability during failover: you should instrument KV hit rate, model variant hit, per-route p95, and cold-start errors. Diego will attach a dashboard example.
[10:27] Diego Ramos: i'll attach a dashboard and an alert runbook. also linking our DR playbook template: https://redwood.example.com/docs/dr-playbook (private link).
[10:36] Priya Patel: thanks, i'll want to edit that template to include our SLA definitions.
[10:41] Sara Lopez: are there any regulatory constraints we should surface for cross-region failover? data residency mostly — some telemetry can be scrubbed but session identifiers can't leave region for certain customers.
[10:53] Diego Ramos: we support geo-fencing policies to prevent specific tenants' traffic from leaving region; for that you must enable regional-only routing in config. if you need full isolation we recommend a private deployment per region.
[11:06] Alice Chen: ok near the end — action items recap and next steps.
[11:12] Tom Müller: also schedule the chaos test and we'll sign off on the test plan.
[11:17] Alice Chen: recap: Diego will draft the DR playbook and cost/latency impact model; Diego will also run a bench and share results; Priya will share traces; Alice will send security docs and the playbook template; Tom to provision test VPC. we'll schedule the chaos test for 2026-05-05.
[11:36] Sara Lopez: thanks all. one small question — are there SLA implications if we enable autoscaling across regions?
[11:43] Diego Ramos: depends on contract; for hosted we have SLOs that consider cross-region failover; for private/dedicated we can negotiate SLA addendum. Alice will loop in sales legal.
[11:55] Alice Chen: thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email and add everything to the shared doc.

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hearings, 'k v' sometimes split. references: DR playbook doc, console prefill API, bench repo.
